newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE-Churches put poverty on NZ election agenda.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Churches put poverty on NZ election agenda.

text.p: New Zealand's conservative government can boast the most vigorous economic recovery in decades as it heads to the polls next month, but critics say it's the poor who have paid the price.
A growth boom since the early nineties has enabled the ruling National Party to increase spending, cut taxes and still build budget surpluses -- a position most countries would envy.
But more people than ever are relying on handouts from charity foodbanks and a recent, highly controversial, study suggested up to one in five New Zealanders may be living below the poverty line.

"Particularly the effect of poverty on children is of real concern -- that we're in danger of perhaps creating an underclass who don't get to participate in the community in a way that we would consider acceptable," says Bonnie Robinson, executive officer with the Council of Christian Social Services.
"They're basically trapped into the edge of society because of poverty and hardship."

Foodbanks, almost non-existent a decade ago, have become a New Zealand institution, with more than 350 spread around the country. "If we weren't there, then the reality is that children and families would go hungry," Robinson said.
Single mother Kasie Whittington, 19, says she has about NZ$50 (US$34.60) a week to buy food for herself and two-year-old Sonja after rent and bills have swallowed up most of her benefits.

"I have my up and down weeks. I may have too many bills one week and have to splash all my money and go to the food pantry," she said. This year she has made "four or five" trips to Wellington's Downtown Community Ministry for canned food, bread, cheese and milk.
Church and welfare groups are asking New Zealanders, whose country helped pioneer the welfare state in the 1930s, to search their consciences as they prepare to vote on October 12.

"Until now, as a nation, we have chosen to tolerate the growth of poverty in our communities. We can equally choose to reverse this trend," a group of Christian churches said in an open letter last month.

Beneath its affluent and harmonious exterior, New Zealand has undergone deep upheaval since the mid-1980s as Labour and then National governments slashed subsidies, dismantled protective trade barriers, tamed trade unions and privatised.
Former Labour Prime Minister David Lange, retiring from parliament at the election, paid tribute in a farewell speech to "those people whose lives were wrecked by us".

And outgoing Governor-General Dame Catherine Tizard caused a political row earlier this year when she spoke of "putting on blinkers and closing our eyes to the misery of those falling into the gutters as we all plough our way on to nirvana".
Fifty-one percent of people believe New Zealand is becoming a worse place to live, according to an opinion poll last week, against just over a third who think it is getting better.
Social Welfare Minister Peter Gresham says he is concerned that more people are using foodbanks.

"Yes, because it's a very difficult culture to reverse, to get back going the other way. There's a degree of use because they're there, they've become a port of call that wasn't necessarily thought of before," he said in an interview.
But the great majority of those receiving state benefits were coping. "There is a fairly well intermeshed system of targeted benefits to meet most circumstances," Gresham said.
National presided over swingeing 1991 cuts in benefits for the unemployed, the sick and single parents, arguing social welfare spending was out of control.
But beneficiaries gained very little from this year's tax cuts, which were deliberately aimed at wage earners in order to get people off welfare and into jobs.
"Underlying all of our programmes is the importance of having a growing economy and the jobs there for people that are seeking them," Gresham said.
The influential Business Roundtable lobby agrees, arguing in a new study that trimming back the welfare state is both morally right and good for social cohesion.

"Those who advocate a halt to policy reforms on the grounds that they may be socially disruptive have failed to recognise that the redistribution state is a fool's paradise -- it promises much but delivers little," the report said.
But critics say the effect has been to punish the poor.

"Those who had their incomes cut because there was a supposed budget blowout (in 1991) have not in fact been the recipients of the supposed recovery when the budget is in surplus," said Jane Kelsey, associate law professor at Auckland University and author of a study of the New Zealand reforms.
"That means that you've got an increasing number of people in the population who are being condemned into long-term poverty unless they can find a way out of the benefit trap."
